title: Information Has Never Been More Plentiful, Yet We Choose Not to Know
dek: Lyse Doucet has reported from war zones for forty years. Her judgment: not knowing isn't because information is scarce, but because we don't want to know. And this Iran war is a war of choice that has made everything worse.
why: The first half offers immediate judgments on Iran and Hormuz; the second half is a rare retrospective on whether twenty years of intervention in Afghanistan was worth it. High information density, but requires patience.
who: Journalists covering the Middle East and Afghanistan, international relations researchers, humanitarian workers, and readers who want to understand the frameworks of "war of choice" and "hope vs. optimism".
skip: The counterfactual speculation after 1:19:53 has lower information density.

points.h: Not knowing is because we don't want to know
points.body: Doucet calls this "a really jarring time": information has never been more plentiful, but "If we don't know about something, it's because we don't want to know about something. We choose not to know." She attributes this to being bombarded daily by statements from the US president—yesterday it was "we don't need guardrails for AI," even as some leading AI founders are asking for regulation; today it's rolling back some environmental regulations. She reminds us: a president who says he won't get involved in "forever wars" still ends up leading the country into them.

points.h: This is a war of choice, and it's getting worse
points.body: Doucet rarely offers personal judgment: this war puts her under great pressure because it is "a war of choice" rather than "a war of necessity," and "it just seems to have made everything worse in every way." She acknowledges that the US and Israel have inflicted massive damage on Iran's military and navy, and Iran's economy is suffering, but strategically "this is a war where President Trump doesn't know how to end it." Iran has not collapsed; the regime is harder than before; promises to protesters have not been kept, and their lives are worse.

Doucet uses inflation to illustrate Iran's predicament: Brits worry about single-digit inflation, "Oh, 4%, oh my God, it's 5%," while Iran is at 82%. She quotes an Iranian woman: I come to the market every day just to watch prices go up; that's how I pass the time. She then juxtaposes Iran and Ukraine—both are "wars of choice" and miscalculations. Trump thought he could go straight through Iran, Putin thought he could go straight through Ukraine, but they found that people's resistance is both creative and determined.

points.h: Iran has weaponized the Strait of Hormuz
points.body: Doucet gives specific mechanisms: the Houthis control the western coast of the Red Sea and the islands in between, claiming not to affect maritime traffic, but the previously de-escalated war between Saudi Arabia and Yemen has reignited; oil prices have risen above $108 a barrel; the Strait of Hormuz is completely deadlocked. Iranians will not let go—they don't just see it as a bargaining chip, but a long-term one. "They've weaponized the Strait of Hormuz." She points out that Trump repeatedly says "I didn't expect them to do this," but anyone who has done war-gaming will tell you that the simulations always quickly lead to Iran controlling Hormuz.

When the Taliban required Afghan women to wear a burqa that leaves only the eyes visible, Afghan women abroad countered that this is not traditional Afghanistan. Doucet points out that the burqa is locally called chadili, with an embroidered mesh; but at the same time, women were also educated at Kabul University. While writing her book, she dug up many old photos and decided she had to tell this history well, so she tracked down a person living in the US—the person's first reaction was "The Intercontinental Hotel, I love that hotel." Their first call lasted four hours; the person drew the hotel's ground floor plan from memory, pointing out which room belonged to the German wife of the mayor of Kabul and which to an Indian.

points.h: Four hours of oral history, six months of silence
points.body: The second call lasted three hours, after which the person disappeared for about six months. The reason lay in Afghanistan's political turmoil: the 1973 kingdom was ended by the first coup, and hotel employees were taken away for questioning—"Why do you work for an American hotel? Are you working for the CIA?" In 1978 came the communist coup, people were thrown into prison, and she had to flee. Happy memories thus dredged up sadness and pain. Finally, Doucet called to ask for permission, and the person said: I cannot appear in your book; it's too sad and too painful for me. Doucet's conclusion: a writer can only get up the next day and find someone else to tell the story, and it will never be told as well.

points.h: Two trillion dollars bought a generation that knows its rights
points.body: Faced with the question "What was it all for?", Doucet admits both sides made mistakes, and this should be a humbling lesson for all NATO allies; there will be a formal review in the future. But she insists it was not in vain: twenty years of international engagement created space for the most educated and connected generation in Afghanistan's history to grow up. She quotes Malala Yousafzai—even reading a book is an act of resistance—and says these girls know their rights, know that Islam gives them the right to education, know that girls around the world go to school while they cannot. "Not enough, but not zero."

points.h: The difference between hope and optimism is agency
points.body: Doucet says she could never distinguish hope from optimism until she read Gordon Brown's "The Future Starts With Us": optimism is wishful thinking, but hope is different because hope carries agency—you don't just wish, you actually work to bring it about. She says she doesn't have the privilege of "not needing to hope"; the agency she has is to fight for Afghan visas, to listen to stories there, and to tell them as well as possible. And everyone has their own bit of agency: some donate, some help girls with online classes, some teach girls in Africa, some help South Sudan, Nicaragua, and some help disadvantaged areas in the UK itself.
